title: The crowded heart of the Hercules globular cluster
caption: The core of the Hercules globular cluster Messier 13, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 13 · constellation Hercules · about 25000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Hubble gives an exceptionally clear look at the core of Messier 13, the great globular cluster in Hercules, where hundreds of thousands of stars crowd together. It is one of the brightest and best-known clusters in the sky, some 25,000 light-years away and about 145 light-years across.

Edmund Halley found it in 1714 and noted that, when the sky is clear and the Moon is absent, it is visible to the naked eye as a little patch. In 1974 the cluster was the target of a symbolic message sent from the Arecibo radio telescope, announcing humanity's existence to anyone who might be listening. More recent studies, though, suggest planets are very rare in the crowded environments of globular clusters.
Kurt Vonnegut wrote about the cluster in his 1959 novel The Sirens of Titan.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.52 x 2.52 arcminutes) and distance (25000 light years), the frame spans roughly 18 × 18 light-years. Its light set out about 25,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: The image combines data from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. A blue filter (F435W) is shown in blue, a red filter (F625W) in green and a near-infrared filter (F814W) shown in red.
understand.eye: Halley saw only a faint patch, but Hubble's long exposures and near-infrared data, invisible to the eye, separate the core into individual stars.

behind.people: See full credit: ESA/Hubble and NASA
behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The image spans about 2.5 arcminutes of sky. Exposure times were 1480 seconds through the blue filter, 380 seconds through the red one and 567 seconds in near-infrared.
alt: The densely packed core of a globular cluster, filled with countless stars.
